title: Make the upgrade mechanism work on Windows, and say what the framework needs to run

history.detail:
PASS: PASS — round 1, with Req 6 recorded as NOT MET and routed, not waved through. Read the Req 6 section before acting on this verdict.

Audited 21dcc8d on top of 13c029b (bookkeeping). Sprint file read fresh immediately before this verdict; `git diff 13c029b HEAD -- docs/sprints/2-in-progress/` is empty, no mid-build amendment. Working tree clean apart from the known-inert .vscode/settings.json.

================================================================
ANSWERING YOUR QUESTION FIRST: BRING IT, AND THE SHAPE IS PASS, NOT CONDITIONAL
================================================================

You asked whether this should have come to me at all, and whether a CONDITIONAL naming just Req 6 is the right shape. Holding the handoff would have been the worst of the three options and I want to be clear why, because the instinct behind it was right and the conclusion wasn't.

Holding it hides a verified fix for a defect that is live right now on every Windows install — the mechanism sprints 6 and 8 built reports success and does nothing there — behind an unrelated question nobody at this gate can answer. That is itself a way of routing around verification: the work that WAS done stops being reviewable because of work that couldn't be.

CONDITIONAL is wrong for a sharper reason. It sends the sprint back to dev_build and names a fix you cannot perform: you cannot conjure a Windows machine from macOS. That is precisely the unclearable precondition this framework has a named rule against — "a precondition must be clearable by the role that hits it, or it must ship with a documented cross-role recovery path." A CONDITIONAL here creates one with no recovery path, and the sprint sits while the live defect stays live.

So: PASS on everything that could be built and verified, Req 6 recorded as an open gap with a named owner. What makes that honest rather than lenient is the routing in the Req 6 section below — without it, a PASS would silently retire a requirement, which is exactly the epic's own failure mode.

And to answer the thing behind your question: declining to guess at Windows behaviour was correct. Req 6 says "test it before changing anything." Changing those paths blind, on three files, on a platform you can't observe, would have been the worse error by a distance.

================================================================
REQ 2 — THE LOAD-BEARING CHECK. PASSES. ROUTES RE-TRACED AND RE-RUN.
================================================================

Normalization changes which KEY is looked up and nothing about what counts as proof. The gate is unchanged:
    proven = recordedHash !== null ? recordedHash === currentHash
                                   : baselineHashesFor(baselines, relPath).includes(currentHash)
toRelPathKey is applied at exactly five places — three lookups (manifestHashFor, baselineHashesFor, baselineHashForVersion), every newManifest write site, and writeManifest itself. It transforms the key argument only. Both routes to overwrite still terminate in an equality between two independently computed sha256 hashes.

Considered and dismissed: could normalization collide two distinct paths onto one key? Only if a shipped filename literally contained a backslash — impossible on Windows, and absent from this package's own paths on POSIX. Even then a collision yields a different file's hash, which cannot equal currentHash. No unearned overwrite is reachable through the key change.

Re-ran the full adversarial matrix against a real published 0.1.2 install, hashing qa1.md before and after each run:
    real baselines, no manifest          overwritten YES, 0 conflicts   (the fix working)
    unparseable baseline table           overwritten NO,  conflict      SAFE
    missing baseline table               overwritten NO,  conflict      SAFE
    baseline table is an array           overwritten NO,  conflict      SAFE
    manifest entry present, wrong hash   overwritten NO,  conflict      SAFE
    stale BACKSLASH-keyed manifest       overwritten YES, 0 conflicts   (see Req 3 — earned, not stale-key)
Sprint 6's and sprint 8's constraints survive intact. No FAIL.

================================================================
REQ 1 — DEMONSTRATED AGAINST THE REAL BASELINE TABLE, NOT READ
================================================================

Reproduced the defect and the fix directly, using the exact string Windows' path.join produces:
    relPath                                 ".claude\\agents\\qa1.md"
    OLD  baselines[relPath]                 undefined          <- the entire sprint 10 defect
    NEW  baselines[toRelPathKey(relPath)]   found, 9 versions  <- fixed
    normalized key                          ".claude/agents/qa1.md"
    CLAUDE.md under the OLD lookup          FOUND
That last line independently confirms the sprint's Context: CLAUDE.md is the one user-owned path with no separator, so it resolved identically with or without normalization, which is why it alone upgraded on Windows and why the observed manifest was {"CLAUDE.md": ...}. The diagnosis in the sprint file is correct, verified rather than accepted.

Normalization is on the lookup side only. scripts/baselines/ is untouched by this commit (empty diffstat) — no published table needs reissuing, which was Req 1's own constraint. Mixed separators and no-separator paths both normalize correctly.

Choosing to replace the literal backslash rather than path.sep is the right call and the comment explains why: keying off path.sep would make the fix untestable anywhere except real Windows, which is exactly how this defect survived three sprints of verification. That reasoning is the most valuable line in the diff.

================================================================
REQ 3 — SETTLED BY INSPECTING BEHAVIOUR, AND I PUSHED IT HARDER THAN ASKED
================================================================

The sprint asks which way this was established. Both: the argument is grounded in the real observed Windows manifest quoted in the Context, and the fallback is tested. I did not rely on either — I built the case that would break it.

Sharp test: a real 0.1.2 install, qa1.md hand-edited so it matches NO published baseline, plus a manifest whose BACKSLASH key carries a hash that correctly matches that customised content. If a stale backslash key could authorize anything, this is where it would fire — the key is "right" about the file's current state.
    result: overwritten NO, sentinel survived, reported as a conflict,
            and qa1.md correctly ABSENT from the resulting 6-key manifest.
A stale backslash key cannot authorize an overwrite under any circumstance: the normalized lookup simply doesn't find it, so it reads as "no manifest entry" and falls through to baselines, where only real published content proves anything. The benign case earlier in the matrix (backslash key + genuinely untouched file → upgraded) is earned by the baseline match, not by the stale key.
Resulting manifests always carry forward-slash keys, so a stale key is dropped rather than round-tripped. Portable between platforms, as Req 1 requires.

================================================================
REQ 4 — BOTH BRANCHES RUN, MESSAGE READ COLD
================================================================

With python3 present: zero warnings. Silent, correct, macOS unchanged.
With no Python on PATH at all (stripped PATH, node only): warns, exit 0, and the files were still written — .claude/agents populated, scripts/run-lifecycle.js and scripts/launcher/python-interpreter.js both present in the target. Never blocks, never silent, as specified.

The message, read as someone on Windows who has never installed Python: it names what is needed (Python 3), where to get it (python.org, and that the Store listing works too), how to check (all three of python3/python/py --version), what a good answer looks like (a "Python 3.x.y" line), and that the install itself succeeded and only the slash commands need this. That is more than the criterion asked for. It passes.

================================================================
REQ 5 — VERIFIED WITH FAKE INTERPRETERS, INCLUDING THE RISK THE SPRINT NAMED
================================================================

Built fake executables on a controlled PATH rather than trusting the unit tests:
    python3 -> prints "Python 2.7.18" on stderr, exit 0
    python  -> prints "Python 3.11.9"
    resolved: python
The Python-2 trap the Risks section names is closed. The check requires the output to start with "Python 3." and reads both streams, which is what catches Python 2's stderr-only --version.

    real machine, python3 present -> resolved: python3. macOS behaviour unchanged.

WORTH RECORDING, because it converts an untested assumption into a non-issue: the comment says Windows' App Execution Alias "exits non-zero rather than printing a version", which is a claim about a platform nobody here can observe. I tested both possibilities — an alias exiting 9009 AND an alias exiting 0 while printing the store message — and both are rejected, because the guard keys on OUTPUT, not exit status. The untested claim is not load-bearing; the code is correct whichever way the alias behaves. That is the right way to write against an unobservable platform.

All 11 Python-backed command files now invoke run-lifecycle.js; sprint-worktree.md is correctly untouched and contains no Python reference; zero command files still hardcode python3, checked in the repo and again in the packed tarball. run-lifecycle.js run end to end: forwards arguments, and forwards a real exit 1 from a failing lifecycle command.

================================================================
REQ 7 / REQ 8 / TARBALL — MET
================================================================

Req 7: package.json 0.1.10, one-line diff.
Req 8: ran it — 87 OK lines, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED. Matches your stated count. All four listed cases present, plus the interpreter-resolution coverage.
verify-tarball.sh: TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED, 0.1.10, launcher files match live source, sprint data clean, baseline table present.

Checked separately, because a new file excluded from the package would ship this whole sprint inert — the exact failure class this epic exists to end:
    scripts/run-lifecycle.js                  IN TARBALL
    scripts/launcher/rel-path-key.js          IN TARBALL
    scripts/launcher/python-interpreter.js    IN TARBALL
    11/12 packed command files invoke run-lifecycle.js, 0 still hardcode python3
run-lifecycle.js is also correctly added to FRAMEWORK_OWNED, so existing installs receive it on upgrade rather than getting new command files that reference a script they don't have.

================================================================
REQ 6 — NOT MET. NOT WAVED THROUGH. THIS NEEDS AN OWNER.
================================================================

Dev Team did not test the /tmp paths on Windows and did not change them. That is the correct behaviour under the requirement's own instruction and I am not marking it against the build. But the requirement is unfulfilled and its acceptance criterion ("confirm this was tested rather than reasoned about") cannot be satisfied by anyone at this gate.

THE ROUTING PROBLEM, WHICH IS THE REAL RISK HERE: Req 6 appears in QA1's criteria, which cannot close it, and appears NOWHERE in LiveQA's criteria — I checked the list. LiveQA's Windows criteria cover the reproduction, the destructive branch, macOS regression, the prerequisite check, and the python.org install. The /tmp question is in neither gate. If this sprint passes both gates as currently written, Req 6 retires unanswered and unrecorded, which is precisely the failure sprint 9's Req 4 exists to prevent, one layer up.

MASTER CONTROLLER: amend LiveQA's criteria to include it. The Windows machine is already a hard dependency of that gate; this is one more thing to type while it is in front of someone. THIS SPRINT SHOULD NOT CLOSE UNTIL REQ 6 IS ANSWERED — /sprint-complete checks the two gates and the user's authorization, not requirement coverage, so nothing mechanical will stop it. That is a decision for the user, made knowingly.

TWO THINGS THE NEXT PERSON WILL NEED, both established here:

  1. REQ 6'S OWN ENUMERATION IS INCOMPLETE. It names /sprint-liveqa, /sprint-abort and /sprint-complete. FIVE command files write to /tmp: those three plus /sprint-new (--title-file, --epic-file) and /sprint-qa1 (--notes-file). Whoever tests this must test all five, not the three named. Grepped, not assumed.

  2. THE EXPOSURE IS BOUNDED, WHICH LOWERS THE URGENCY WITHOUT CLOSING THE QUESTION. Every affected flag has an inline alternative already in the parser — --notes, --user-said, --reason, --title, --epic. A Windows user who hits this has a working path today; nothing tells them so, which is the actual gap.

MY OWN ATTEMPT, LABELLED AS REASONING NOT TESTING, per the boundary this project just added to master-controller.md — which applies to me too. I cannot close this, but I can narrow it, and "unknown" was doing more work than it needed to. On Windows a leading "/" means the root of the current drive, so Python's open("/tmp/x") resolves to <drive>:\tmp\x, which does not exist by default. That gives two distinct failure shapes rather than one unknown: under cmd/PowerShell both writer and reader agree on C:\tmp and it fails only because the directory is absent (a mkdir away); under Git Bash the shell maps /tmp to an MSYS temp directory while Python still reads C:\tmp, so the two disagree and the file is silently not found. The second is the nastier one and is the likelier configuration for anyone running this on Windows. That is a hypothesis for whoever has the machine, not a finding, and I am recording it as such rather than as an answer.

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL
================================================================

1. THE SPRINT 9 RESHIP GAP RECURRED, ONCE, AS PREDICTED. Sprint 9's notes flagged that npm's version immutability forces a bump when a fix must reach the registry mid-fix-loop, and that pipeman.md step 9's trigger (a version bump "in the sprint's requirements") would not fire for it. Commits 87d9f55 ("bump to 0.1.9 — 0.1.8 is already published, npm forbids a republish") and c519ab4 are that scenario, one sprint later. Master Controller's own stated threshold is that a recurrence after a sprint ships is the evidence for a mechanical gate. This is recurrence number one, on the record, so nobody has to rediscover the mechanism.

2. THE BASELINE TABLE IS ONE RELEASE STALE AGAIN. It now covers 0.1.0-0.1.8 (regenerated 2026-09-01, good — someone acted on sprint 9's note), but 0.1.9 is published and absent, and nothing in the release process re-runs the generator. It does not bite this sprint, and I verified that rather than assuming it: every tracked user-owned file is byte-identical between published 0.1.8 and 0.1.9, so a 0.1.9 install's content still matches a table row. That is luck, not design — had sprint 9's reship touched an agent file, every Windows 0.1.9 install would still conflict after this fix, which is the exact population this sprint exists to rescue. Sprint 10 changes no user-owned file either, so 0.1.10 is also covered. The systemic fix is one line in pipeman.md's release order.

3. Both new launcher modules are single-purpose, exported, and unit-tested — which is the only reason this fix is verifiable at all from macOS. Extracting them rather than inlining was the decision that made this sprint auditable.

CODE QUALITY

Test coverage: 87 passing; the toRelPathKey tests use manually-constructed Windows-shaped strings, and the interpreter tests use real fake executables on a controlled PATH rather than mocks.
Error handling: findPython3Interpreter never throws — every failure folds to "try the next, then null". run-lifecycle.js handles spawn error and the signal case (status null -> exit 1) rather than exiting 0 and claiming success.
Standards: shared modules rather than duplicated logic in eleven command files; run-lifecycle.js correctly added to FRAMEWORK_OWNED; comments explain why, including why path.sep was rejected.
Security: the destructive branch is unchanged and re-verified closed across six adversarial cases.
Reporting accuracy: the count was right, and you caught and corrected your own "all twelve" error before committing. Noted, because for four sprints running it was the reports that were wrong, not the code, and that has now stopped.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 10, then Pipeman ships --commit 21dcc8d specifically, using sprint 9's ordering — verify-tarball with the state write uncommitted, publish, then commit the bookkeeping.

Then, before this sprint closes: Master Controller amends LiveQA's criteria to carry Req 6, and LiveQA answers it on the Windows machine along with everything else. If no Windows machine is available when this reaches the live gate, the sprint file's own instruction stands and is correct — record nothing and say so. A macOS pass on this sprint would be worse than no verdict.

PASS: LIVE-LOOP AUDIT RECORD (not a gate-1 verdict — see below). Sprint 10, phase liveqa_live. Re-read the current sprint file fresh, including the uncommitted amendment. Build unchanged: 21dcc8d's tree is 5e1b88982b41e6ae9360e61a3f80ae9937c2379e, byte-identical to the qa1_audited_tree_hash recorded at round 1. Nothing in scripts/ or .claude/ has moved.

WHY THIS IS A LIVE-LOOP RECORD AND NOT THE FRESH GATE-1 PASS THAT WAS REQUESTED

The handoff asks for a fresh /sprint-qa1 10 so the sign-off attests to the amended file, and describes the path as "cmd_qa1 accepts dev_agreed_done, so this is the documented path rather than a workaround: re-audit -> /sprint-dev-done again -> ship."

Two premises there are wrong, and I checked before acting rather than after.

  1. SPRINT 10 IS NOT AT dev_agreed_done. It is at liveqa_live. It has already shipped (40663f8) and published.
  2. AT liveqa_live, /sprint-qa1 CANNOT PRODUCE A GATE-1 VERDICT. cmd_qa1's first branch is
     `if state["phase"] in LIVEQA_PHASES: _qa1_live_loop_audit(args, state); return` — sprint 7's
     live-loop path. It is append-only by construction: it writes one history event and nothing else.
     It never sets qa1_audit_result, never sets qa1_audit_file_hash, never sets qa1_audited_tree_hash,
     never moves phase. I verified that exhaustively in sprint 7's own audit across eight separate
     inputs, and the whole point of building it that way was that a live-loop audit can never refresh
     or launder a gate-1 verdict.

So running /sprint-qa1 10 here does not and cannot re-stamp the sprint-file hash. It records this. The mechanism is working exactly as specified; the plan was written against a phase the sprint has already left.

AND THE REST OF THE PLAN IS MOOT FOR THE SAME REASON. /sprint-dev-done 10 cannot run again from liveqa_live, and there is nothing left to ship — Pipeman already shipped and published. There is no gate between here and LiveQA's verdict for a refreshed hash to guard.

WHICH MEANS THE STALE HASH GUARDS NOTHING NOW, AND NO GATE WAS BYPASSED. Worth stating plainly, because the concern behind the request was legitimate. At round 1 the recorded hash matched the file as it then stood; dev-done checked it and passed; ship checked the tree and passed. The amendment landed after all three. The hash gate did its job at every point it was consulted. What it cannot do is retroactively re-attest, and it was never designed to.

THE AMENDMENT ITSELF — AUDITED, NO FINDINGS

Confined entirely to the LiveQA criteria section: six added lines, nothing removed, no Requirement, no QA1 criterion, no Out of Scope item touched. Gate 1's subject matter is the code and QA1's own criteria, and neither moved. Diffed the whole file rather than trusting the section heading.

It is a better amendment than what I recommended, in three specific ways:
  - The five-file enumeration is correct. I grepped it independently: sprint-abort.md, sprint-complete.md,
    sprint-qa1.md, sprint-new.md, sprint-liveqa.md. Exactly those five, and singling out sprint-qa1 as
    the one that matters most is right — it runs every sprint, for every team.
  - My Git Bash reasoning is labeled as a hypothesis, with "Do not record the hypothesis as the result."
    That is the correct handling of it and it is what I asked for. I offered it as a narrowing, not a
    finding, and it is carried as exactly that.
  - It adds a decision I did not think to ask for and would have: the determination is the deliverable,
    the fix is not, and a broken /tmp does NOT fail this sprint. The reasoning is sound — a code change
    discovered at gate 2 would force a re-audit and re-ship for a defect that predates this release.
    That converts an open question into something LiveQA can actually close in one pass.
  - Pointing out that /sprint-liveqa --notes-file on this very sprint IS the test is the cheapest
    possible way to run it. No extra scenario to construct.

No new findings. Nothing here changes my round-1 PASS on the build, and nothing here needed to.

BLOCKING FOR LIVEQA, THOUGH: THE AMENDMENT IS UNCOMMITTED

`git status` shows the sprint file modified in the working tree only. The last commit touching it is 13c029b — sprint start. Six insertions exist nowhere in history.

LiveQA is about to be handed criteria that live in one working tree and nowhere else, on a sprint whose whole Req 6 exists because something "existed only in a chat log until now." Commit it before LiveQA runs. That is not pedantry about process; it is the same failure this sprint is already carrying a requirement about.

A FINDING THAT IS NOT ABOUT THIS AMENDMENT, AND MATTERS MORE THAN IT

last_shipped_commit is 6c1fc67, not 21dcc8d. The handoff tells Pipeman "the audited commit is still 21dcc8d and its tree still matches; whatever you publish from must leave gitHead matching last_shipped_commit without a post-hoc correction." But 20daca7 is titled "Correct sprint 10's shipped-commit record to 6c1fc67" — the post-hoc correction the instruction forbids has already happened, and last_shipped_commit holds its result.

The cause is structural, not a mistake by Pipeman, and it is a real gap in sprint 9's Req 1 that three sprints of work did not close:
    21dcc8d   the audited commit (tree 5e1b8898..., matches qa1_audited_tree_hash)
    6c1fc67   "Record sprint 10 round 1 QA1 PASS and dev-agreed-done"  <- DEV TEAM's bookkeeping
    40663f8   "Ship sprint 10 (commit 21dcc8d)"                        <- Pipeman's bookkeeping
Sprint 9's reorder moves PIPEMAN's bookkeeping commit after the publish. It does nothing about DEV TEAM's PASS/dev-done bookkeeping commit, which necessarily lands on top of the audited commit before Pipeman is ever invoked. So HEAD at publish time was 6c1fc67, npm stamped that as gitHead, and the record had to be corrected to match reality.

cmd_ship did not catch it because it compares the tree of the commit Pipeman explicitly names, not HEAD — which is correct behaviour and is why the gate held. But npm stamps HEAD. The two cannot agree unless HEAD at publish time IS the audited commit, and Dev Team's own bookkeeping commit guarantees it is not.

I flagged the adjacent version of this in sprints 9 and 10 ("if bookkeeping lands on top first, HEAD moves") and it turns out the consequence is not that ship refuses — it is that the publish silently stamps the wrong commit and someone corrects the record afterward. That is the exact outcome sprint 9's Req 1 was built to eliminate, occurring on the release immediately after it shipped.

FOR MASTER CONTROLLER: this is a second, independent instance of the publish-record class (the first being 8f597b8, which sprint 11's Req 11 fixed). It is not fixed by "package.json changed since the last ship" — that trigger decides WHETHER to publish, not what HEAD is when you do. The candidate fixes all belong upstream of Pipeman: Dev Team holds the PASS/dev-done bookkeeping commit until after the publish, the same way Pipeman now holds its own; or Pipeman publishes from a detached checkout of the audited commit. Both are decisions, not this sprint's work, and I am not proposing one here. Recording the mechanism so nobody has to rediscover it a third time.

WHAT I RECOMMEND

1. Commit the amendment. LiveQA cannot be handed criteria that exist only in a working tree.
2. Do not run /sprint-dev-done 10 or hand Pipeman a fresh ship. Both are already done; neither transition
   is available from liveqa_live, and the audited tree still matches the commit that actually shipped's
   predecessor either way.
3. Accept this live-loop record as what the phase allows: QA1 has re-read the amended file and has no
   findings. If a gate-1 verdict that literally hashes the current file is wanted, the only honest way
   to get one is a new sprint, and that is not worth doing for six added lines in the other gate's section.
4. LiveQA proceeds on the amended criteria, and answers Req 6 on both shells.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.1.10 on BOTH platforms: a real Windows 11 ARM VM (the criteria that matter) and macOS (the no-regression criterion). Environment: Windows 11 26100 ARM64, node v24.20.0, npm 12.0.2, Python 3.13.14 (Microsoft Store install), PowerShell 5.1 and Git Bash MINGW64; macOS Darwin arm64. 2026-09-03.

THE WINDOWS RUN HAPPENED. The sprint file said this gate "CANNOT be satisfied on macOS" and that LiveQA should record nothing if no Windows machine was available. Before accepting that, I checked — per sprint 9's Req 4, which forbids asserting untestability without attempting it — and found a Windows 11 ARM VM on this very machine. It is encrypted, so the user unlocked and booted it and ran the suites; I authored them and scored the output. Every Windows result below is from that VM running the published artifact from the npm registry, not from a simulation.

PROVENANCE — VERIFIED
`npm view fully-completely version` -> 0.1.10; `npm view fully-completely@0.1.10 gitHead` -> 6c1fc67acb47e813d7cc4623b2ce783279fc5f69, an exact match for last_shipped_commit. Registry confirmed live from inside the Windows VM as well: 0.1.10.

Pipeman flagged that gitHead is not the raw audited commit (21dcc8d) because two bookkeeping commits from other sessions sharing the checkout landed between push and publish. I verified rather than accepted this: QA1's recorded qa1_audited_tree_hash is 5e1b88982b41e6ae9360e61a3f80ae9937c2379e and `git rev-parse 21dcc8d^{tree}` is identical; `git diff --name-only 21dcc8d 6c1fc67 -- ':!docs/sprints'` is EMPTY. Nothing unaudited shipped. The disclosure was accurate.

================================================================
CRITERION 1 — 0.1.10 ON THE REGISTRY, gitHead MATCHES: PASS. Covered above.
================================================================

================================================================
CRITERION 2 — THE REVERSED REPRODUCTION, ON WINDOWS: PASS. THIS IS THE SPRINT.
================================================================
Clean Windows install of published 0.1.2 into C:\Users\cehob\fc10-repro, nothing customised, upgraded to published 0.1.10.

Result: "Upgraded 0.1.2 -> 0.1.10", EXITCODE=0, and **ZERO conflicts**. All six agent files AND CLAUDE.md were Replaced with backups written:
  .claude\agents\dev-team-1.md, dev-team-2.md, liveqa.md, master-controller.md, pipeman.md, qa1.md
  CLAUDE.md
each with its own .fc-bak-0.1.2. 23 files replaced in total, 23 backups confirmed present on disk.

On 0.1.9 this exact scenario produced six false conflicts and upgraded nothing. The mechanism sprints 6 and 8 built is no longer inert on Windows.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT — the manifest written on Windows contains seven entries and every key uses FORWARD SLASHES:
  ".claude/agents/dev-team-1.md", ".claude/agents/dev-team-2.md", ".claude/agents/liveqa.md",
  ".claude/agents/master-controller.md", ".claude/agents/pipeman.md", ".claude/agents/qa1.md", "CLAUDE.md"
Not a backslash anywhere. Req 1's normalization works on the platform it was written for, and manifests are portable between platforms as specified. Before this release the same file held exactly one entry, {"CLAUDE.md": ...}, because CLAUDE.md is the only user-owned path without a separator.

The rules genuinely arrived, not merely the files: qa1.md contains "demonstrated, not argued" (count 1) and CLAUDE.md contains "Transition-precondition design rule" (count 1). Both were absent in 0.1.2. This is the epic's goal reaching a Windows install for the first time.

================================================================
CRITERION 3 — THE DESTRUCTIVE BRANCH, ON WINDOWS: PASS. FIRST REAL TEST OF IT THERE.
================================================================
The sprint file notes this passed on 0.1.9 for the wrong reason — nothing was ever overwritten because nothing ever matched. With matching now working, this is the first time the branch has been genuinely exercised on Windows.

Installed published 0.1.4 (marker 0.1.4; manifest absent, confirmed, i.e. the true pre-manifest shape), planted SENTINEL-S10-WINDOWS-MUST-SURVIVE in .claude\agents\qa1.md, upgraded to 0.1.10.

  PRE-UPGRADE  qa1.md sha256 = FC11DCE3B99E982661F108EFCD6558493BAFF2F467E5B76FE11B15BAAD867B92
  POST-UPGRADE qa1.md sha256 = FC11DCE3B99E982661F108EFCD6558493BAFF2F467E5B76FE11B15BAAD867B92
  SENTINEL COUNT = 1
  RESULT: SAFE - file NOT overwritten
Exactly ONE conflict was reported, naming .claude\agents\qa1.md, and no qa1.md.fc-bak-* was written. Meanwhile the five untouched agent files and CLAUDE.md were correctly recognised and handled.

The manifest for that target holds SIX entries with qa1.md ABSENT. The edited file matched neither a manifest entry nor a published baseline, so it was not proven untouched, so it was neither upgraded nor recorded. Normalization changed which key is looked up and did not change what counts as proof, exactly as Req 2 requires. Sprint 6's Req 3 and sprint 8's Req 1 are intact on Windows.

================================================================
CRITERION 4 — macOS UNAFFECTED: PASS
================================================================
Ran 0.1.2 -> 0.1.9 and 0.1.2 -> 0.1.10 side by side on macOS. Identical on every dimension that matters: 0 conflicts both, 7 user-owned files replaced both, 7 manifest entries both, exit 0 both, manifest keys forward-slash. The Replaced count rises from 12 to 23 solely because 0.1.10 also ships the twelve rewritten slash commands and the new launcher modules — I confirmed the extra files are exactly those rather than assuming it. No platform was fixed by breaking the other.

Additional macOS checks of the Windows-motivated logic, run because the requirements have macOS-verifiable components even though the defects do not:
 - Req 5 fallback chain: with python3 removed from PATH and only `python` present — the python.org install shape — the new scripts/run-lifecycle.js shim resolved it and ran correctly.
 - Req 5 with no interpreter at all: clean error naming python3/python/py, where to get Python, and how to verify.
 - Req 2/Req 3 safety on macOS: sentinel in a 0.1.4 install survived (hash identical, excluded from manifest).
 - Req 3's migration question, which the sprint asked to establish rather than assume: I planted a stale BACKSLASH manifest key whose hash matched an EDITED file — the case that would be destructive if backslash keys were ever honoured. REQ 6's DETERMINATION — ESTABLISHED ON BOTH SHELLS, AND QA1's HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED
================================================================
QA1's labelled hypothesis was: cmd/PowerShell likely works unless C:\tmp is absent, while Git Bash likely fails silently. Instructed to confirm or refute by running, and not to record the hypothesis as the result. The real answer is close to the reverse, and neither shell fails silently.

POWERSHELL — FAILS, LOUDLY. C:\tmp does not exist on a default Windows box (confirmed: "C:\tmp exists? False"). Writing to /tmp failed first ("Out-File : Could not find a part of the path 'C:\tmp\liveqa-notes.txt'"), and the real command then died with an unhandled Python traceback ending:
  FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '\\tmp\\liveqa-notes.txt'
  EXITCODE=1
`status --verbose` afterwards confirmed nothing was recorded: Phase still dev_build, "QA1 audit result: None (rounds: 0)". So no corruption and no silent success — but on a default Windows box in PowerShell, following the command files as written is impossible.

GIT BASH — WORKS, AND THE NOTES LAND. `cygpath -w /tmp` resolves to C:\Users\cehob\AppData\Local\Temp, not C:\tmp, and MSYS translates the argument on the way to Python. The real command succeeded: "QA1 audit PASSED (round 1)", exit 0. Critically, `status --verbose` proves the note was stored verbatim rather than recorded empty:
  [2026-09-03T16:22:39+00:00] qa1: audit PASS: probe notes written from git bash
The relative-path control also passed (round 2), isolating /tmp as the only variable. The silent-empty-record failure mode QA1 was most worried about does not occur.

SCOPE OF THE POWERSHELL PROBLEM: five command files instruct writing to /tmp — sprint-abort, sprint-complete, sprint-qa1, sprint-new, sprint-liveqa. sprint-qa1 runs on every sprint for every team. On Windows/PowerShell none of them can record via --notes-file without the user first creating C:\tmp by hand.

Per the sprint file this determination is the deliverable and the fix is not, and it explicitly does not fail this sprint — the defect predates this release and a code change discovered at gate 2 would force a re-audit and re-ship. Recording it as a follow-up. Master Controller now has a real answer on both shells rather than a hypothesis, including the fact that the hypothesis was wrong in both directions.

================================================================
Windows renders the installer's em dashes as "ΓÇö", e.g. "Conflicts ΓÇö left untouched, review by hand (1):" and inside the conflict message itself.

I nearly reported this from the first run and did not, because that upload arrived as ISO-8859 and the corruption could have been my own capture pipeline. I re-captured with explicit UTF-8 encoding; the second upload is genuine UTF-8 and still shows "ΓÇö". Decoding UTF-8 E2 80 94 (em dash) as CP437, the default Windows console codepage, produces exactly "ΓÇö". So this is the Windows console, not my transport.

Cosmetic, not functional — no behaviour depends on it. Worth recording because it is the same class of defect as this sprint's subject: invisible on macOS, visible to every Windows user, and it lands in the conflict message and the Python-prerequisite warning, i.e. the two messages whose entire job is telling a confused user what to do. ================================================================

TWO HARNESS BUGS OF MY OWN, RECORDED SO THE RESULTS ARE READ CORRECTLY. First, my PowerShell suite contained em dashes; PowerShell 5.1 read the BOM-less UTF-8 file as Windows-1252, where byte 0x94 is a smart closing quote, which terminated a string early and made the whole file unparseable.
